signals: find two elements that add up to target
return indices, not values
exactly one solution / any order
unsorted array with a pair condition
complement lookup: need x such that target - x was seen
constraints: n up to 1e4 makes O(n^2) borderline-passable but the intended solution is O(n); values up to 1e9 in magnitude mean you cannot index an array by value, so use a hash map keyed by value.
confusable: Sorting plus two pointers is tempting because it works for the value pair, but sorting destroys the original indices you must return; the hash map keeps index information for free.
variants: If the array is sorted and you must return positions, use two pointers (167 Two Sum II)
If you need all unique triplets or quadruplets summing to a target, sort and fix elements then two-pointer (15 3Sum, 18 4Sum)
If it becomes a stream of numbers with repeated queries, keep the hash map as a class (170 Two Sum III)

signals: digits stored in a linked list, reverse order
add / sum two numbers represented as lists or strings
carry across positions
two sequences walked together with possibly different lengths
construct a new list while consuming inputs
constraints: At most 100 nodes per list, so complexity is a non-issue; the constraint is really that the number can be arbitrarily large, so converting to an integer is meant to be disallowed and you must simulate digit-by-digit with a carry.
confusable: Converting each list to an integer, adding, and converting back looks easiest but fails on languages with fixed-width ints and misses the point; the intended pattern is a dummy-head merge-like walk with carry.
variants: If digits are stored most-significant first, reverse the lists or use stacks (445 Add Two Numbers II)
If the inputs are strings of digits, same carry loop from the right end (415 Add Strings)
If the number is stored as an array and you add 1, the carry loop degenerates to propagate a single carry (66 Plus One)

signals: longest substring / contiguous subarray
without repeating / at most k distinct / no duplicates
a window validity condition that only gets worse when you extend and better when you shrink
need last seen index of each character
length of best window, not the window itself
constraints: n up to 5e4 rules out O(n^2) substring enumeration; the window with a char to last-index map runs in O(n). The alphabet is letters, digits, symbols and spaces, so use a dict or a 128-slot array, not a 26-slot one.
confusable: Brute force over all substrings with a set check is the beginner move and is O(n^2) or worse; also watch that the left pointer must never move backwards when the stale duplicate index is before the current left.
variants: If it becomes at most k distinct characters, count frequencies in a map and shrink while distinct count > k (340 Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters)
If you may replace up to k characters to make them all the same, window is valid while length - maxFreq <= k (424 Longest Repeating Character Replacement)
If the subarray must contain all characters of another string, it becomes a minimum window (76 Minimum Window Substring)

signals: palindromic substring
longest / count palindromes
symmetric around a center
substring must be contiguous (not subsequence)
n small enough for quadratic
constraints: n up to 1000 permits O(n^2) expand-around-center or O(n^2) DP; O(n^3) brute force would be about 1e9 and too slow. If n were 1e5 you would need Manacher's algorithm.
confusable: Longest common substring of s and reversed s looks equivalent but is wrong when a reversed non-palindrome copy exists elsewhere in the string; and beginners confuse this with palindromic subsequence, which is interval DP, not center expansion.
variants: If asked to count palindromic substrings, the same center expansion counts each successful extension (647 Palindromic Substrings)
If it becomes longest palindromic subsequence, that is interval DP on dp[i][j] (516)
If you must reach O(n), use Manacher's algorithm; if you must partition into palindromes, precompute the palindrome table then backtrack or DP (131, 132)

signals: digits stored in a linked list, reverse order
add / sum two numbers represented as lists or strings
carry across positions
two sequences walked together with possibly different lengths
construct a new list while consuming inputs
constraints: At most 100 nodes per list, so complexity is a non-issue; the constraint is really that the number can be arbitrarily large, so converting to an integer is meant to be disallowed and you must simulate digit-by-digit with a carry.
confusable: Converting each list to an integer, adding, and converting back looks easiest but fails on languages with fixed-width ints and misses the point; the intended pattern is a dummy-head merge-like walk with carry.
variants: If digits are stored most-significant first, reverse the lists or use stacks (445 Add Two Numbers II)
If the inputs are strings of digits, same carry loop from the right end (415 Add Strings)
If the number is stored as an array and you add 1, the carry loop degenerates to propagate a single carry (66 Plus One)

signals: written in a pattern then read row by row / line by line
convert / rearrange characters according to a described layout
direction that bounces between two bounds
only the row (or bucket) each element lands in matters
simulate the walk rather than compute the geometry
constraints: n and numRows up to 1000, so a single O(n) pass appending to numRows buckets is plenty; a 2D grid of size numRows by n would be 1e6 cells, wasteful but still passable, which is why a bucket per row is the intended simplification. Watch the numRows == 1 edge case where the direction never flips.
confusable: Building the actual 2D zigzag grid with columns is the beginner move and is fiddly; only the row index sequence 0,1,..,r-1,r-2,..,1,0 matters, so bucket by row.
variants: If the output required a fixed period formula instead of simulation, index by i mod (2*numRows-2)
If it were a spiral instead of a zigzag, simulate with direction vectors and boundary shrinking (54 Spiral Matrix, 59 Spiral Matrix II)
If characters had to be reshaped into a diagonal traversal, bucket by i+j (1424 Diagonal Traverse II)

signals: reverse digits / manipulate digits of an integer
32-bit signed range, return 0 on overflow
cannot use 64-bit integers
peel digits with mod 10 and div 10
check overflow before the multiply, not after
constraints: Input is a single 32-bit int so there is no complexity question; the constraint that you cannot store 64-bit values is the whole problem, forcing a pre-multiplication check against 2^31-1 div 10 and its last digit.
confusable: Converting to a string, reversing, and casting is the obvious route but sidesteps the overflow rule; in Python it silently works, but the interview-intended solution checks rev > (2^31-1)//10 before rev*10.
variants: If asked whether a number reads the same reversed, reverse only half the digits (9 Palindrome Number)
If asked to parse digits from a string with sign and clamping, same overflow guard plus whitespace and sign handling (8 String to Integer atoi)
If digit manipulation is on a very large number, treat it as a string or list of digits (66 Plus One)

signals: choose two positions to maximize width times min(height)
pair of lines / walls / endpoints
area or product where one side limits the answer
start from the widest and shrink
greedy elimination: moving the taller side can never help
constraints: n up to 1e5 rules out checking all O(n^2) pairs (5e9); the two-pointer scan is O(n). Heights up to 1e4 and n up to 1e5 keep area within 1e9, so no overflow concern in most languages.
confusable: It looks like Trapping Rain Water (42) because of the water metaphor, but here water is only between the two chosen lines, not accumulated across bars; and brute-force pairs time out.
variants: If water is trapped over every bar, use two pointers tracking left and right max, or a monotonic stack (42 Trapping Rain Water)
If the two chosen elements must satisfy a sum condition instead of a product, sorted two pointers (167 Two Sum II)
If you want the largest rectangle under a histogram rather than between two walls, use a monotonic stack (84)

signals: all triplets that sum to zero / target
solution set must not contain duplicates
unsorted array, return values not indices
fix one element then reduce to two sum
k-sum family
constraints: n up to 3000 permits O(n^2) which is 9e6 operations; O(n^3) brute force is 2.7e10 and fails. Sorting is allowed because values (not indices) are returned, and sorting makes duplicate skipping trivial.
confusable: Hash-map two sum inside a loop works but makes deduplication painful and needs extra sets; sort first so that duplicate triplets are adjacent and can be skipped by comparing neighbors.
variants: If it becomes four numbers, add another fixed loop (18 4Sum) or generalize to k-sum recursion
If asked for the triplet sum closest to a target, keep the best absolute difference while moving pointers (16 3Sum Closest)
If asked to count triplets with sum less than target, on each pointer move add right-left to the count (259 3Sum Smaller)

signals: all unique quadruplets / k numbers summing to target
distinct indices, return values in any order
must avoid duplicate results
fix elements with nested loops then two pointers
k-sum family
constraints: n up to 200 makes O(n^3) about 8e6, which is fine, so two fixed loops plus a two-pointer pass is the intended complexity; values and target up to 1e9 mean sums can reach 4e9 and overflow 32-bit ints in some languages.
confusable: Reusing the 3Sum hash approach or a hash of pair sums gets deduplication wrong (same pair used twice or duplicate quadruplets); sort and skip equal neighbors instead.
variants: If there are four separate arrays and you count index tuples, hash all pair sums of the first two arrays (454 4Sum II)
If it is three numbers, drop one loop (15 3Sum)
If k is a parameter, write a recursive kSum that bottoms out in two pointers

signals: n-th node from the end
one pass / without knowing length
linked list where you need a position relative to the tail
delete a node so you need the node before it
gap of n between two pointers
constraints: At most 30 nodes so any approach passes; the implicit constraint is the follow-up demanding a single pass, which forces the two-pointer gap technique instead of count-then-walk.
confusable: Counting the length and walking again is correct but two passes; also, forgetting the dummy head breaks the case where the head itself is removed (n equals length).
variants: If asked for the middle node, use slow/fast where fast moves two steps (876 Middle of the Linked List)
If asked whether the list has a cycle or where it starts, that is the same fast/slow machinery (141, 142)
If asked to rotate the list by k, find length, connect tail to head, and cut at length - k mod length (61 Rotate List)

signals: brackets / parentheses must be matched and properly nested
open must be closed in correct order
last opened, first closed
validate a string of delimiters
matching pairs of different types
constraints: n up to 1e4 with a single O(n) stack pass; stack depth can reach n, so recursion-based matching would be risky but an explicit stack is fine.
confusable: Counting opens minus closes works only for a single bracket type; with multiple types ordering matters, and a counter cannot detect ([)] so a stack is required.
variants: If only one bracket type and you need the minimum insertions or removals to make it valid, a counter suffices (921, 1249)
If you must find the longest valid substring, use a stack of indices or a counter scanning both directions (32 Longest Valid Parentheses)
If the string is an expression to evaluate, the stack holds operands and operators instead (150, 224, 227)

signals: merge two sorted lists / arrays
splice nodes together, return a single sorted sequence
the merge step of merge sort
two pointers advancing over two sorted inputs
dummy head to build output
constraints: At most 50 nodes per list; the O(m+n) merge is the intended and only sensible complexity. Sorted input is the hint: you never need to compare more than the two current heads.
confusable: Collecting all values, sorting, and rebuilding is O((m+n) log(m+n)) and ignores the sortedness and the splice-the-nodes requirement; the merge walk is linear.
variants: If there are k lists, merge with a min-heap or pairwise divide and conquer (23 Merge k Sorted Lists)
If the inputs are arrays and one has spare capacity, merge from the back (88 Merge Sorted Array)
If you must sort a linked list from scratch, split with slow/fast and merge (148 Sort List)

signals: k sorted lists / arrays / streams to combine
repeatedly need the smallest among k current candidates
k-way merge
total elements N with k sources
sorted inputs plus more than two of them
constraints: Total elements up to 1e4 and k up to 1e4; merging one list at a time is O(N*k) = 1e8 which is borderline, while a heap or divide-and-conquer gives O(N log k). Empty lists (length 0, k up to 0) must be skipped when seeding the heap.
confusable: Repeatedly merging list i into an accumulator like 21 looks natural but is O(N*k); the heap holding one head per list, or pairwise merging in log k rounds, is the intended improvement.
variants: If asked for the k-th smallest element in a sorted matrix, same heap of row heads (378) or binary search on value
If asked for the smallest range covering one element from each of k lists, heap plus track current max (632 Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists)
If only two lists, plain merge (21); if inputs are arrays, the same heap over (value, listIndex, elementIndex)

signals: swap adjacent nodes / reorder nodes in fixed-size groups
may not modify node values, only pointers
linked list rewiring with a fixed group size
need prev, first, second, next pointers
dummy head to handle the first group
constraints: At most 100 nodes, so a single O(n) pass with O(1) extra space is all that is asked; the real constraint is the ban on swapping values, which forces pointer surgery.
confusable: Swapping the values in the two nodes passes the tests but violates the stated rule; recursion is also clean here but for k-groups iterative rewiring is expected.
variants: If the group size is k instead of 2, reverse each full group in place (25 Reverse Nodes in k-Group)
If you must reverse a sub-range given by positions, walk to the node before and reverse a fixed count (92 Reverse Linked List II)
If you must interleave the first half with the reversed second half, split, reverse, merge (143 Reorder List)

signals: reverse k at a time / in groups of k
leftover nodes remain as is
cannot change node values, only nodes
linked list segment reversal repeated
need to check a full group exists before reversing
constraints: n up to 5000 with k up to n; O(n) with O(1) extra space is expected, and the group check must not re-scan more than k nodes per group so the total remains linear.
confusable: Reversing the whole list and fixing up afterwards, or copying values into an array and writing them back, is either wrong for partial groups or breaks the no-value-change rule; do a bounded reverse per group with reconnection.
variants: If k equals 2, it is Swap Nodes in Pairs (24)
If you reverse only one range given by positions left and right, it is Reverse Linked List II (92)
If groups alternate between reversed and untouched, add a toggle between groups (Reverse Alternate k Nodes, a common interview variant)

signals: first occurrence of needle in haystack
substring search / pattern matching / indexOf
return index or -1
fixed-length pattern compared at each position
string matching family
constraints: Both lengths up to 1e4, so the naive O(n*m) slide is up to 1e8 character comparisons in the worst case and still passes; KMP or rolling hash gives O(n+m) and is what a follow-up would expect.
confusable: Trying a variable-size sliding window with character counts finds anagrams, not exact matches; the pattern must match in order, so compare slices or use KMP.
variants: If you need to find all anagram positions of the pattern, fixed window with frequency counts (438 Find All Anagrams in a String)
If you must handle many queries or very long strings, Rabin-Karp rolling hash (187 Repeated DNA Sequences) or KMP failure table (1392 Longest Happy Prefix)
If you check whether one string is a rotation of another, search s1 in s2+s2

signals: substring that is a concatenation of all words in any order
all words have the same length
exact multiset match of chunks
window of fixed total length = wordLen * count
start offsets modulo word length
constraints: s up to 1e4, up to 5000 words of length up to 30; checking each of the n start positions by chopping into count chunks is O(n * count) ~ 5e7 with early bailout, acceptable. The optimized version slides one window per starting offset in [0, wordLen), giving O(n * wordLen).
confusable: A character-frequency sliding window (like anagram search) is wrong because chunks must be whole words in the given alignment; and generating all permutations of words is factorial.
variants: If words were single characters, it becomes Find All Anagrams (438) with a fixed window
If words had different lengths, you would need a Trie or backtracking (word break style, 139/140)
If you need the minimum window containing a multiset of characters rather than an exact concatenation, use 76 Minimum Window Substring

signals: sorted then rotated / pivoted
O(log n) required
find target in an array with one discontinuity
one half of any split is always sorted
distinct values
constraints: n up to 5000 would technically pass a linear scan, but the statement demands O(log n); distinct values are what guarantee that comparing nums[mid] with nums[lo] tells you which half is sorted.
confusable: Plain binary search on nums fails because the array is not globally sorted; finding the rotation point first works but is two searches, while checking which half is sorted at each step is a single search.
variants: If duplicates are allowed, you may have to shrink both ends by one when nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi], degrading to O(n) worst case (81 Search in Rotated Sorted Array II)
If asked for the minimum, binary search comparing mid to hi (153, 154)
If the array is unimodal instead of rotated, binary search for a peak (162 Find Peak Element, 852)

signals: validate a board / grid against row, column and sub-box rules
no repetition within a group
fixed 9 x 9 size
membership test per group
group key derived from (r//3, c//3)
constraints: The board is fixed at 81 cells so complexity is irrelevant; the design question is the data structure, and sets keyed by row, column, and box index (or a 9x9 bitmask) give O(1) checks in a single pass.
confusable: Trying to actually solve the puzzle is unnecessary and much harder; also, checking only rows and columns and forgetting the 3x3 boxes is the common bug.
variants: If asked to fill the board, backtrack with the same three set families (37 Sudoku Solver)
If asked whether N queens are placed validly, use sets for columns and the two diagonals r-c and r+c (51 N-Queens)
If validating a matrix where each row and column must be a permutation, same per-row and per-column sets (2133 Check if Every Row and Column Contains All Numbers)

signals: fill empty cells subject to constraints
exactly one solution guaranteed
try each candidate, recurse, undo
constraint satisfaction on a small fixed board
backtracking with O(1) validity checks
constraints: Fixed 9 x 9 board, so the search space, not n, is the concern; with row/col/box sets making each check O(1) and pruning on the first conflict, plain backtracking is fast enough. The unique-solution guarantee means you can stop at the first success.
confusable: Treating it as pure validation (36) or trying a greedy fill-cells-with-a-single-candidate loop stalls on harder boards; you need recursion with undo.
variants: If placing N non-attacking queens, same backtracking with column and diagonal sets (51/52 N-Queens)
If filling a grid path with all cells visited, backtracking with visited marking (980 Unique Paths III)
If the choices per step are letters instead of digits, it becomes Word Search (79)

signals: return all combinations / all unique combinations
sum to target
same number may be chosen unlimited times
distinct candidates
enumerate subsets with a start index to avoid permutations
constraints: At most 30 candidates, values 2..40 and target up to 40, so combinations have at most 20 elements and the tree is small; the exponential enumeration is intended. Sorting candidates and breaking when a candidate exceeds the remaining target prunes heavily.
confusable: Coin-change DP counts or minimizes but cannot list the combinations; also, iterating from index 0 in the recursion produces permutations and duplicate combinations, so pass a start index.
variants: If each candidate may be used at most once and there are duplicates, sort and skip equal siblings at the same depth (40 Combination Sum II)
If only the count of combinations is needed, use DP (518 Coin Change II) or minimum coins DP (322)
If you need k numbers from 1..9 with a target, bounded backtracking (216 Combination Sum III)

signals: minimum number of jumps / steps
each position gives a maximum reach forward
fewest moves to reach the end
BFS layers over a line
current level's farthest reach
constraints: n up to 1e4 so an O(n^2) DP (for each i, relax all reachable j) is 1e8 in the worst case and usually passes, but the greedy level-by-level scan is O(n). Reachability is guaranteed, so you never need a failure branch.
confusable: Greedy jump to the largest nums[i] fails because a smaller jump can land on a better launch pad; the correct greedy jumps to whichever position maximizes i + nums[i] within the current range, which is BFS by levels.
variants: If asked only whether the end is reachable, track the maximum reach (55 Jump Game)
If jumps can go both directions or cost varies, this becomes a real BFS or DP (1306 Jump Game III, 1345 Jump Game IV)
If each jump has a cost or a score, use DP with a monotonic deque for the window max (1696 Jump Game VI)

signals: rotate matrix 90 degrees
in-place, do not allocate another matrix
n x n square grid
transpose and reverse
layer by layer four-way cycle
constraints: n up to 20 so time is not a concern; the in-place requirement is the entire problem and forces either transpose-then-reverse-rows or moving four cells at a time with one temp.
confusable: Writing rotated[j][n-1-i] = matrix[i][j] into a fresh matrix is easy but violates in-place; and an incorrect composition (reverse then transpose) gives counter-clockwise rotation.
variants: If rotation is counter-clockwise, transpose then reverse each column (or reverse rows then transpose)
If the matrix is not square, in-place is impossible, so you must allocate (867 Transpose Matrix)
If you traverse in a spiral rather than rotate, use shrinking boundaries (54 Spiral Matrix)

signals: group / bucket items by some equivalence
anagrams: same letters, different order
canonical key for each item
return groups in any order
hash map from key to list
constraints: Up to 1e4 strings of length up to 100; sorting each string costs O(L log L) for total ~7e6, and a 26-count tuple key gives O(L) per string. Lowercase-only letters make the 26-slot count tuple possible.
confusable: Comparing every pair of strings for anagram-ness is O(n^2 * L) = 1e10; the insight is to compute a canonical form once per string and bucket, not to compare pairs.
variants: If checking whether two strings are anagrams, compare counts directly (242 Valid Anagram)
If grouping strings by shift pattern instead of letter multiset, the key becomes the sequence of differences mod 26 (249 Group Shifted Strings)
If finding all anagram occurrences inside a text, use a fixed sliding window of counts (438)

signals: can you reach the last index
each element is the maximum jump length
reachability along a line
farthest reach so far
greedy on a prefix
constraints: n up to 1e4 so an O(n^2) DP would be 1e8 and borderline; the intended O(n) greedy tracks the farthest reachable index (or scans right to left for the leftmost good index). Values up to 1e5 exceed n, so cap reach at n-1 or just compare.
confusable: DFS/BFS over all reachable positions works but is quadratic or exponential without care; since reach on a line is contiguous, a single max-reach variable suffices.
variants: If asked for the minimum number of jumps, use the level-by-level greedy (45 Jump Game II)
If you can jump either direction by exactly nums[i] and need to reach a zero, real BFS with visited (1306 Jump Game III)
If the array is a circular track or has costs, model as a graph or DP (1345, 1696)

signals: intervals with start and end
merge overlapping
return non-overlapping set that covers all
sort by start then sweep
overlap only with the last kept interval
constraints: Up to 1e4 intervals so O(n log n) sort plus linear sweep is intended; O(n^2) pairwise overlap checks would pass here but do not generalize. Coordinates up to 1e4 would even allow a difference array but sorting is the general tool.
confusable: Checking each interval against all previously merged ones is O(n^2) and unnecessary; after sorting by start, an interval can only overlap the most recently merged one.
variants: If a single new interval must be inserted into an already sorted non-overlapping list, three-phase scan (57 Insert Interval)
If asked how many intervals to remove so none overlap, sort by end and greedily keep (435 Non-overlapping Intervals)
If asked for the minimum number of rooms or the maximum overlap, sweep line with events or a min-heap of end times (253 Meeting Rooms II)

signals: already sorted non-overlapping intervals
insert one new interval and merge if necessary
three regions: before, overlapping, after
two intervals overlap if they share a point
output remains sorted
constraints: Up to 1e4 intervals already sorted, so a single O(n) pass is intended; re-sorting and running Merge Intervals would be O(n log n) and acceptable, but wastes the given order.
confusable: Appending the new interval and calling Merge Intervals (56) works but ignores the sorted guarantee; also, using strict inequality for overlap misses intervals that touch at a single point.
variants: If many intervals must be inserted or the set changes dynamically, keep a sorted structure or TreeMap (715 Range Module)
If instead you remove an interval from a set, split intervals that straddle it (1272 Remove Interval)
If the intervals are unsorted, sort first and merge (56)

signals: grid path from top-left to bottom-right
move only right or down
minimize / maximize / count paths
cell value depends on top and left neighbours
non-negative weights
constraints: m, n up to 200 so an O(m*n) = 4e4 DP is trivial; the restricted movement (right/down only) is what makes it DP rather than Dijkstra, since the DAG order is row-major.
confusable: Greedy choosing the smaller of right and down at each step fails because a locally cheap step can lead into an expensive region; and running Dijkstra is correct but overkill when moves are only right and down.
variants: If you only count the paths (with or without obstacles), same DP with addition (62 Unique Paths, 63 Unique Paths II)
If movement is allowed in all four directions, it becomes Dijkstra or 0-1 BFS (1631 Path With Minimum Effort, 1368)
If the grid is a triangle, same DP with two parents per cell (120 Triangle)

signals: integer square root / rounded down
cannot use built-in pow or sqrt
find the largest k with f(k) <= x where f is monotonic
binary search on the answer
single integer input up to 2^31-1
constraints: x up to 2^31-1 so a linear scan of ~4.6e4 candidates would pass, but the monotonic predicate mid*mid <= x is the hint for O(log x) binary search; mid*mid can reach ~4.6e18, so use 64-bit or compare mid <= x // mid.
confusable: Reaching for Newton's method or floating point sqrt then flooring can be off by one for large x; binary search on integers is exact.
variants: If asked whether x is a perfect square, same search but require mid*mid == x (367 Valid Perfect Square)
If asked for the k-th root or the smallest divisor satisfying a bound, binary search on the answer with a monotonic feasibility check (1283, 875 Koko Eating Bananas)
If computing pow(x, n), use fast exponentiation instead (50 Pow(x, n))

signals: number of distinct ways to reach
each step choose 1 or 2
count paths / ways on a line
answer for n depends on n-1 and n-2
Fibonacci-shaped recurrence
constraints: n up to 45 keeps the answer within 32-bit (fib(46) ~ 1.8e9), which is why 45 was chosen; O(n) DP with two rolling variables is expected, and plain recursion is 2^45 and times out.
confusable: Enumerating actual sequences with backtracking explodes exponentially; only the count is asked, so use the recurrence.
variants: If each step has a cost and you minimize, dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]) (746 Min Cost Climbing Stairs)
If you can climb up to k steps or specific step sizes, sum over the allowed sizes (like 377 Combination Sum IV)
If you must cover a board with tiles of two shapes, the same linear recurrence with different coefficients (790 Domino and Tromino Tiling)

signals: canonical path / normalize
'..' goes up one level
tokens that undo the previous token
split on a delimiter and process sequentially
stack of components
constraints: Path length up to 3000, so split and a single O(n) stack pass is all that is needed; tricky inputs like '/../', '//' and '/a/./b/../../c/' matter more than size.
confusable: String replace tricks on '/./' and '/../' fail on repeated or nested cases; a stack of directory names handles '..' popping correctly, including popping an empty stack at root.
variants: If the tokens are operations that cancel each other (e.g., 'C' removes the last score), same stack (682 Baseball Game)
If adjacent equal characters cancel, stack-based removal (1047 Remove All Adjacent Duplicates in String)
If comparing two typed strings with backspaces, a stack or a reverse two-pointer walk (844 Backspace String Compare)

signals: minimum window / smallest substring
contains all characters of t including duplicates
expand until valid, shrink while valid
frequency map of required characters
need counter that tracks how many characters are satisfied
constraints: m, n up to 1e5 rules out O(m^2) window enumeration; the two-pointer window is O(m + n). Letters only, so a 52- or 128-slot array works, but a dict is fine. Track a 'formed' counter so validity is O(1) per step, not a full map comparison.
confusable: Comparing the whole frequency map at each step makes it O(m * alphabet) which is fine here but sloppy; the real trap is a fixed-size window (anagram search) when the window length is not known in advance.
variants: If the window must be exactly the length of t, use a fixed-size window (438 Find All Anagrams, 567 Permutation in String)
If asked for the longest window with at most k distinct characters, flip the expand/shrink condition (340)
If it becomes a subsequence rather than substring, use two pointers or DP (727 Minimum Window Subsequence)

signals: does a word exist in a grid
adjacent cells horizontally or vertically
each cell used at most once
path search with restore on backtrack
small grid, moderate word length
constraints: Grid at most 6 x 6 and word up to 15, so exponential DFS from every cell is intended; mark visited in place and restore. If the grid were large or there were many words, you would need pruning or a Trie.
confusable: Plain BFS or DFS with a global visited set fails because different paths may reuse the same cell; visited must be per path, i.e., marked and unmarked as you backtrack.
variants: If there are many words to find, build a Trie and DFS once from each cell (212 Word Search II)
If you need the number of islands or connected regions instead of a specific path, flood fill with a global visited set (200)
If the target is a path visiting every cell, count with backtracking (980 Unique Paths III)

signals: sorted linked list
delete duplicates so each value appears once
duplicates are adjacent
compare node with next
in-place rewiring
constraints: At most 300 nodes; the sorted guarantee means a single O(n) pass with no extra memory, whereas an unsorted list would require a hash set.
confusable: Reaching for a set of seen values is unnecessary given the sort; and confusing this with 82, which removes every node that has a duplicate rather than keeping one copy.
variants: If nodes with duplicates must be removed entirely, keep a prev pointer and skip whole runs (82 Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II)
If the input is a sorted array and must be done in place, two pointers write and read (26 Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array)
If the list is unsorted, use a hash set of seen values

signals: largest rectangle / area in a histogram
for each bar, nearest smaller to the left and right
width of bars, contiguous span limited by a shorter bar
next smaller element
monotonic increasing stack
constraints: n up to 1e5 rules out O(n^2) expanding from each bar; the monotonic stack computes each bar's left and right boundary in amortized O(1). Heights up to 1e4 times width 1e5 gives 1e9, fine in 32-bit but close.
confusable: Two pointers from the ends (like Container With Most Water) is wrong because the rectangle must be filled by all bars in between, not just bounded by two; you need nearest-smaller boundaries.
variants: If the histogram is built row by row from a binary matrix, run this per row (85 Maximal Rectangle)
If asked for next greater element instead of next smaller, flip the stack comparison (496, 503)
If the goal is trapping water rather than a rectangle, use the stack on decreasing heights or two-pointer max tracking (42)

signals: reverse a sub-range of a linked list
positions left and right, 1-indexed
reverse in one pass
need the node before the segment and the node after
stitch reversed segment back in
constraints: n up to 500 with left <= right <= n; O(n) single pass, O(1) space is expected. left can be 1, so a dummy head is needed to have a node before the segment.
confusable: Reversing the whole list and trying to fix the boundaries afterwards is wrong; or copying values to an array and writing back reverses values rather than nodes, which passes but misses the pointer skill.
variants: If you reverse the entire list, this collapses to 206 Reverse Linked List
If you reverse every k nodes, repeat this segment reversal (25 Reverse Nodes in k-Group)
If you reverse only even or odd positioned groups, add a counter to decide which segments to reverse

signals: inorder / preorder / postorder traversal
return node values in traversal order
BST sorted order equals inorder
iterative with explicit stack
left, node, right
constraints: At most 100 nodes so recursion is safe; the iterative stack version is worth knowing because the follow-up asks for it and because deep trees (1e4+) can overflow recursion in some languages.
confusable: Using a queue gives level order, not inorder; and in the iterative version, pushing right before visiting the node instead of walking left first gives preorder.
variants: If you need the k-th smallest in a BST, run inorder and stop at k (230 Kth Smallest Element in a BST)
If you need O(1) space, Morris traversal with threaded pointers
If you need a next() iterator over a BST, keep the inorder stack as object state (173 BST Iterator)

signals: return all structurally unique trees / all structures
BST on values 1..n
choose each value as root, combine left and right results
cartesian product of subproblem results
enumerate all solutions, not count
constraints: n up to 8 gives Catalan(8) = 1430 trees, so the output itself is exponential and enumeration is intended; memoizing on (lo, hi) ranges avoids recomputing shared subtrees.
confusable: The counting version (96) uses DP on sizes, but here you must return actual trees, so DP on sizes is not enough; you need the value ranges to build nodes.
variants: If only the count is required, use the Catalan recurrence (96 Unique Binary Search Trees)
If enumerating all full binary trees with n nodes, same split-and-combine recursion (894 All Possible Full Binary Trees)
If enumerating all ways to parenthesize an expression, same divide by each operator (241 Different Ways to Add Parentheses)

signals: bi-directional / undirected graph given as edge list
is there a path from source to destination
connectivity / same component
vertices labeled 0..n-1
reachability query
constraints: n and edges up to 2e5, so O(n + E) BFS/DFS or near-linear union-find is required; adjacency matrix (4e10) is impossible, and recursive DFS may overflow the stack on a long path so prefer iterative or union-find.
confusable: Treating the edges as a tree or scanning edges once without building adjacency misses multi-hop paths; you must build an adjacency list or union the endpoints.
variants: If there are many connectivity queries, union-find answers each in near O(1) (1971 itself, or 547 Number of Provinces)
If you need the shortest path length in an unweighted graph, BFS with distance (1091 Shortest Path in Binary Matrix)
If you must count components, DFS from every unvisited node or count union-find roots (323 Number of Connected Components)

signals: count structurally unique BSTs / trees
values 1..n, choose root splits into left and right sizes
count(n) = sum count(i-1)*count(n-i)
Catalan numbers
count, not enumerate
constraints: n up to 19 keeps Catalan(19) = 1.7e9 inside a 32-bit int; O(n^2) DP is trivial and naive recursion without memo is exponential. The small n is a hint that the answer grows fast and only counting is expected.
confusable: Trying to enumerate the trees (95) times out for n = 19 and is unnecessary; the shape count depends only on subtree sizes, not on the values themselves.
variants: If you must return the trees, recurse on value ranges (95 Unique Binary Search Trees II)
If counting valid parenthesis strings, matching bracket sequences or full binary trees, it is the same Catalan recurrence
If asked for the number of ways to reorder an array to give the same BST, it becomes combinatorics with binomials (1569)

signals: valid BST / all left keys strictly less, right strictly greater
whole subtree must satisfy a bound, not just the child
pass down (lower, upper) bounds
inorder must be strictly increasing
tree property with global (not local) constraint
constraints: Up to 1e4 nodes and values spanning the full 32-bit range, so bounds must use None or infinity sentinels rather than INT_MIN/INT_MAX; O(n) recursion depth up to 1e4 is fine in most settings but an iterative inorder is safer.
confusable: Checking only node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val passes locally but misses a grandchild that violates an ancestor's bound; the bound must propagate from every ancestor.
variants: If asked to find the two swapped nodes in a BST, use inorder and look for descents (99 Recover Binary Search Tree)
If asked for the k-th smallest, inorder traversal (230)
If the property is a max-heap or balanced height instead, recursion returns height or a boolean up the tree (110 Balanced Binary Tree)

signals: two trees identical / structurally the same
compare two roots node by node
both null, one null, values differ
recursive structural equality
two trees walked in lockstep
constraints: At most 100 nodes so recursion is trivially fine; the pattern is the base-case ladder (both None, one None, values differ) followed by recursion on both children.
confusable: Comparing traversal outputs (e.g., inorder lists) is insufficient because different shapes can produce the same sequence; compare structure and values together.
variants: If asked whether a tree is a mirror of itself, compare left and right subtrees as mirrors (101 Symmetric Tree)
If asked whether one tree is a subtree of another, run same-tree at every node (572 Subtree of Another Tree)
If asked whether two trees are leaf-similar, compare only leaf sequences (872)

signals: mirror of itself / symmetric around center
compare left subtree with right subtree
left.left vs right.right, left.right vs right.left
structural equality with swapped children
two subtrees walked in mirror lockstep
constraints: At most 1000 nodes so recursion is fine; an iterative version pushes pairs of nodes onto a queue or stack and is worth knowing for the follow-up.
confusable: Checking that inorder traversal is a palindrome fails on shapes that differ but produce palindromic sequences; compare the two subtrees as mirror images.
variants: If comparing two separate trees for equality, drop the mirror swap (100 Same Tree)
If asked to invert a tree, swap children recursively (226 Invert Binary Tree)
If asked whether two trees are flip-equivalent (any child swaps allowed), recurse on both mirrored and non-mirrored pairings (951)

signals: level order / level by level / breadth-first
list of lists grouped by depth
queue where you process the current queue size as one level
left to right within a level
shortest distance in an unweighted structure
constraints: Up to 2000 nodes, so O(n) BFS with a queue is straightforward; the trick is snapshotting len(queue) at the start of each level so levels are grouped correctly.
confusable: DFS with a depth parameter also works if you index the output by depth, but beginners try inorder or preorder and cannot recover level boundaries.
variants: If alternating direction per level, reverse every other level (103 Zigzag Level Order)
If you need the rightmost node per level, take the last element of each level (199 Binary Tree Right Side View)
If you need level averages, maxima, or the bottom-up order, same BFS with a different reduction (637, 515, 107)

signals: zigzag / alternate direction per level
level order with a twist
left to right then right to left
toggle flag per level
BFS with post-processing
constraints: Up to 2000 nodes, so O(n) BFS plus reversing alternate level lists is fine; a deque appending at alternating ends avoids the reversal but is not required at this size.
confusable: Trying to alternate the traversal order of children in the queue itself corrupts later levels; keep BFS normal and reverse the output list for odd levels.
variants: If no alternation, it is plain level order (102)
If you must return levels bottom-up, reverse the outer list (107)
If you need the widest level with positional gaps, carry index labels through BFS (662 Maximum Width of Binary Tree)

signals: maximum depth / height of a tree
longest root-to-leaf path in nodes
1 plus max of subtree answers
empty tree returns 0
post-order style aggregate
constraints: Up to 1e4 nodes, so recursion depth can reach 1e4 on a degenerate tree; Python's default limit is 1000, so an iterative BFS counting levels or an explicit stack is safer.
confusable: Minimum depth is not the mirror image: a node with one child must not count the missing child as a leaf (111 Minimum Depth), and beginners copy the max formula and get it wrong.
variants: If asked for minimum depth, BFS to the first leaf or handle single-child nodes specially (111)
If asked whether the tree is height-balanced, return height and a flag together (110)
If asked for the longest path between any two nodes, combine left and right depths at each node (543 Diameter of Binary Tree)
